text.content:
The
Shepherd's
Transit

(Gm Only)

This scenario is not about winning a firefight. It is about what the patrol chooses to care about when time runs out. To make this tangible, track variables such as Local Trust and Command. These can shift visibly with a +1/-1 marking, representing the impact of decisions made under pressure. A recommended method for tracking Trust and Command is to use tally marks on index cards or a dedicated section on a whiteboard, allowing for easy updates and visibility. This tracking ensures that player choices regarding what they prioritize or neglect are not only meaningful but also clearly reflected in the narrative progression of the ecosystem.

The patrol is deliberately placed between:

  • Mission success

  • Civilian obligation

  • Mission success

  • Enemy manipulation. While approaching the zone, players might notice fresh tire ruts leading off the main road and discarded food wrappers, suggesting recent enemy movement and preparation. These details signal the enemy’s timeline without direct GM narration.

Prepare events, not answers.

Time:

Pre-dawn

Condition:

Quiet, routine, tense but uneventful

“Shepherd One, Qalat Actual. Copy SP complete. No new reporting since last patrol. Maintain planned timeline. Call when approaching CP1. Over.”

We mount up in the dark, the kind that dulls depth and sharpens sound. Engines idle low, a constant vibration through the armored hulls as you climb inside, boots scraping metal floors already dusted with sand. Doors slam shut in sequence and the convoy eases forward, blacked-out headlights, shadows stretching long and uncertain beyond the wire. The fort falls away behind us, generators and Hesco fading into silhouettes as the MSR opens up, narrow and pale under the first hint of morning light.

The drive is quiet, radios mostly silent except for short checks and acknowledgments. Fields slide past on either side, flat and open, broken by irrigation ditches and low walls that seem too deliberate to ignore. Nothing moves, yet everything feels watched. As the sky lightens, the road ahead becomes clearer, but that only makes the emptiness more unsettling. This stretch is familiar to the maps and foreign to the gut, and every kilometer closer to CP1 feels like crossing an invisible line you won’t get to uncross.

Nothing happens. This is deliberate. Let that quiet moment stretch out, building tension. The lull is not just an absence but a prelude, a waiting silence that seems to hold its breath. Then, faintly crackling through the radio, a distant intercept picks up a snippet of chatter.

The patrol reaches CP1.

CP1 announces itself more by instinct than landmarks—a subtle bend, a change in ground texture, the sense that this is where someone once decided to stop and look. The vehicles slow and halt, engines idling as dismounts step out into the cool morning air. Helmets tilt, eyes scan, and small movements are made to look casual. It feels like a pause taken on borrowed time, the kind that stretches just long enough to make you aware of how exposed you really are.

While the rest of the patrol lingers, adjusting straps and shifting weight, the snipers slip away without ceremony. They move low and deliberate, using shallow folds in the land and sparse vegetation that only works if you trust it. There’s no signal, no goodbye—just the quiet understanding that they are now somewhere you cannot see. When the patrol remounts, the ground where the snipers vanished looks no different than it did before, which somehow makes it worse.

“Specter, Shepherd Two. Insert now. Same rules as briefed. Minimal traffic. You are eyes only unless it goes bad. Report anything that looks like intent. Over.”

“Shepherd One, Specter. GHOSTRIDER set. Good hide. Comms may be intermittent. We’ll call what we see. Out.”

Sniper insertion should be disguised:

  • Short halt.

  • Troops dismount casually.

  • Snipers fade into the terrain.

  • Vehicles remount and depart.

Once inserted, the sniper team goes dark.

Trigger Phase 3 exactly once, when any occur:

  • Patrol leaves CP1

  • GM judgment: momentum is slipping

Do not delay this for pacing. This is the pivot point of the scenario.

(the following is for Dilemma 3 details on next page)

You roll out from CP1 with the sense that something important has been left behind, even though you know exactly where the snipers are supposed to be. The mirrors catch one last glimpse of scrub and low ground before the road straightens again, pulling your attention forward. The light is stronger now, washing color back into the landscape, but it does nothing to soften the tension that settles in once CP1 is behind you.

Ten minutes down the MSR, the scene appears abruptly, like it was waiting just out of sight. A child lies slumped in a wooden wheelbarrow, blood soaking into the dirt beneath her, one leg mangled beyond anything natural. An older man grips the handles for a heartbeat too long, eyes wide and panicked, then releases them and runs, fast and clumsy, disappearing into the fields without looking back. The air feels heavy here, close and wrong, and the silence drags. Every moment of indecision weighs heavily, as if the clock itself were counting down.

Procedure

  1. @UUID[Compendium.outside-the-wire.macros.Macro.0gItG585Lvxnmy04]{Roll 1d10 on the Civilian Dilemma Table}

  2. Read one paragraph of the Situation aloud (no elaboration)

  3. Start a real-world 60-second timer

  4. Ask once: “What do you do, Patrol Leader?”

A: @UUID[Compendium.outside-the-wire.macros.Macro.0gItG585Lvxnmy04]{The Dilemma Table (1d10)}

1-2. Bleeding Passenger

Situation: A civilian pickup has pulled onto the shoulder. Inside is a wounded passenger bleeding heavily from the leg. The driver is frantic. No weapons visible. No obvious IED indicators.

Pressure:

  • Stopping delays the VIP timeline

  • Leaving is visible to witnesses

Likely Consequences (GM/Solo):

  • Aid → [[/tracker "local trust" +1]]{+1 Trust}, Timeline breaks

  • Ignore → [[/tracker "local trust" -1]]{-1 Trust}, Command +0

  • Half-measures → [[/tracker "command confidence" -1]]{-1 command}

3-4. Blocked Road

Situation: A farm vehicle has jackknifed across the MSR. Several civilians are attempting to move it. The road cannot be cleared quickly without assistance or heavy vehicles.

Pressure:

  • Clearing it exposes the patrol

  • Forcing through risks of civilian harm

Likely Consequences:

  • Assist → [[/tracker "local trust" +1]]{+1 Trust}, [[/tracker "sunlight clock" +1]]{+1 Sunlight}

  • Push through → [[/tracker "local trust" -1]]{-1 Trust}

  • Detour → [[/tracker "insurgent activity" +1]]{+1 Insurgent Activity}

5-6. Injured Child

Situation: A child lies wounded near the road, trauma consistent with an IED blast. A man flees as you approach. No immediate threats detected.

Pressure:

  • Medical aid breaks mission timing

  • Ignoring causes visible harm

Likely Consequences:

  • Aid → [[/tracker "local trust" +1]]{+1 Trust}, VIP missed

  • Ignore → [[/tracker "local trust" -1]]{-1 Trust}

  • Secure & call locals → [[/tracker [[/tracker "local trust" +1]]{+1 Trust}

7-8. Civilian Mob

Situation: A growing group of civilians moves toward the patrol, shouting and gesturing at the road ahead. Emotions are high. You cannot tell if the anger is directed at you or something beyond the bend.

Pressure:

  • Stopping risks loss of control

  • Pushing through risks escalation

Likely Consequences:

  • De-escalate → [[/tracker "local trust" +1]]{+1 Trust}, Delay

  • Force movement → Command +0, [[/tracker "local trust" -1]]{-1 Trust}

  • Withdraw → [[/tracker "insurgent activity" +1]]{+1 Insurgent Activity}

9-10. Flaming Donkey

Situation: A teen is holding an upset donkey by the reins in the middle of the road. Behind them lay an overturned cart with its contents of vegetables splayed across the road. Somehow, the donkey’s tail is on fire, causing the donkey to buck and scream wildly. In the nearby fields, workers watch the scene.

Pressure:

  • Helping diverts manpower

  • Ignoring undermines legitimacy

Likely Consequences:

  • Assist → [[/tracker "local trust" +1]]{+1 Trust}, [[/tracker "sunlight clock" +1]]{+1 Sunlight}

  • Ignore → [[/tracker "local trust" -1]]{-1 Trust}, Command +0

B: When the timer ends

  • If no decision → [[/tracker "command confidence" -1]]{-1 command} and [[/tracker "local trust" -1]]{-1 Trust} immediately

  • Then force a choice

No re-briefs. No recap. No hints.

Decision Limits
(Anti-Analysis Rule)

Players may:

  • Choose one primary action

  • Assign one secondary task

They may not:

  • Split the patrol into more than two elements

  • Call higher for guidance

  • Attempt “perfect coverage” solutions

If they try: “You don’t have the time or assets for that.”

BASIC TRAINING

How to Resolve Checks

STEP 1: Roll 2d10 and add them together

STEP 2: Compare with your Ability

Example: Your First Aid is 15

Your roll of 11 vs. First Aid 15

STEP 3: Determine Success or Failure

Roll Equal to or Under your Ability = SUCCESS ✓

Roll Over your Ability = FAILURE ✗

Fast Resolution (No Scene Drag)

Resolve the dilemma with at most one roll:

  • Medical / De-escalation → First Aid or Civil Affairs

  • Suspicion / Investigation → Instinct

  • Forcing movement → Tactics

On:

  • Success → Apply benefit, still advance time

  • Failure → Apply consequence + escalate later

No retries. No extended play.

CRITICAL RESULTS

Natural 2 = CRITICAL SUCCESS

Exceptional result, maximum effect

Natural 20 = CRITICAL FAILURE

Catastrophic result, worst possible outcome

DIFFICULTY ROLL MODIFIERS

Apply these modifiers to your Roll before measuring against your Ability (Instinct):

Very Easy -5: to your roll

Example: 11 Roll becomes a 6 for this check

Easy: -2 to your Roll

Example: 11 Roll becomes 9 for this check

Average: 0 to your Roll

Tricky: +2 to your Roll

Example: Roll of 11 becomes 13 for this check

Hard: +5 to your Roll

Example: Roll of 11 becomes 16 for this check (failure)

Immediate Consequences

Apply one now, not abstractly:

Choice Type

Immediate Effect

Aid Civilians

[[/tracker [[/tracker "local trust" +1]]{+1 Trust}, VIP timeline broken

Ignore Civilians

[[/tracker "local trust" -1]]{-1 Trust}, morale fracture

Force Through

[[/tracker "local trust" -1]]{-1 Trust}, visible anger

Detour

[[/tracker "sunlight clock" +1]]{+1 Sunlight}, Insurgent reposition

Over-engineer

[[/tracker "command confidence" -1]]{-1 command} automatically

Do not hide these effects. Tell players what just shifted.

Enemy Response
(Fast & Visible)

If any delay occurred:

  • During Phase 4, automatically:

    • Insurgents gain a better position

    • Ambush geometry improves

    • Snipers report earlier than expected setup

No roll required. This keeps the scenario on schedule.

GM Safety Rails (Important)

  • Do not escalate lethality here

  • Do not punish empathy with death

  • Punish time loss, attention loss, and predictability

The harm comes later.

The radio crackles once, then again, sharp and urgent against the steady engine noise. When the sniper’s voice comes through, it’s low and controlled, but there’s an edge to it you haven’t heard before. Earlier whispers hinted at the Colonel’s early departure from another source, but you dismissed it as noise. Now, as snipers report movement near CP1, describing fighters deliberately setting up rather than passing through, it becomes clear the situation requires immediate tactical responses. You picture the ground in your mind as the report unfolds: motorcycles pulled in tight, men moving with purpose, and machine guns emplaced to cover the road. This isn’t noise; it’s preparation. Consider these potential courses of action: reroute the patrol to avoid the line of fire or stage a tactical feint to mislead the enemy while another team flanks their position. These options can spur strategic brainstorming and creative solutions in the face of imminent threats.

As the transmission continues, the picture sharpens in uncomfortable ways. The ambush is angled toward the most obvious CASEVAC route, the kind of thinking that assumes someone will get hurt—and soon. The snipers watch it come together piece by piece, knowing exactly what it means and feeling powerless to stop it from their hide. The road behind you suddenly feels longer, heavier, like it’s tilting downhill toward something already in motion.

Regardless of the patrol’s choice with the wounded child, the snipers report:

  • Insurgents are establishing an ambush near CP1.

  • Likely oriented on the most logical CASEVAC route players return route to Fort Qalat.

  • Enemy strength: 8 fighters on four motorcycles.

  • Equipment: PKMs, surface-laid IEDs, motorcycles

  • Players (Sniper) need to roll against their tactical to see if their hide site remains hidden. This is an Easy roll (-5), since the Insurgents are not looking for them.

Regular Insurgents

Combat Cell • Moderate Threat

THREAT ASSESSMENT

Threat Level: MODERATE

• Dressed in local garb — blend with the population until engagement

• Armed with AK-pattern rifles, 2-3 magazines

• Arrive in two sedans — mobile, can quickly reinforce or withdraw

• Better trained: Small Arms (9), Heavy Weapons (8)

• Civil Affairs (7) and Explosives (5) — can set IEDs

EQUIPMENT

AK-Pattern Rifle • 2-3 Magazines • Local Clothing • Two Sedans (transportation)

ABILITIES

Prowess 7 • Instinct 6 • Tactics 6 Small Arms 9 • Heavy Weapons 8 • Explosives 5

SITREP

“Shepherd One… Specter. Traffic picked up near CP1. Fighters moving with purpose, not transiting. Machine gun in play. Possible IED prep along MSR. This looks deliberate. Recommend reassessment. Over.”

(Pause. Let players react.)
Then immediately:

FROM: COMPANY A / COLONEL (CUTTING IN)

“Shepherd One, this is Alpha Actual. We’re adjusting movement. I want this route reassessed before I move. Turn your patrol around and return to CP1. We’ll bring the principal to you. Acknowledge.”

Should the players try to argue.

“Negative delay, Shepherd. This is standard escort doctrine. We do not push VIPs into uncertainty. Secure CP1. We’ll meet you there.”

Critical Insight (GM Only):

The insurgents believe the Colonel is already moving. The normal procedure for traveling with a VIP is not to stop and engage, not to place the VIP at risk, but to press forward to the next CP. Upon arrival, assess damages and casualties.

The sudden, jarring turn back toward Checkpoint 1 felt like a violation of the day’s fragile routine, and the landscape itself began to reflect the escalating tension. The patrol leader’s eyes, already straining, caught movement in the distance: entire families, not just individuals, were leaving the Main Supply Route, their carts and bags being pulled quickly off the road and into the low fields—a clear, unsettling sign that the local population knew exactly where the fight was about to be.

This mass exfiltration coincided with the flickering presence of the enemy’s eyes: small, agile motorcycle scouts, moving in short, aggressive bursts. They’d shoot past the patrol’s flanks and then pull in tight to the vegetation, leapfrogging the convoy with brazen confidence, using the patrol’s own movement and the civilian exodus to maintain distance and report on the herd’s progress, a chilling confirmation that the patrol was not hunting, but being actively driven into the waiting trap.

  • When Patrol Returns Toward CP1, the Patrol Leader must make a Tactics check - hard (+5), they are not expecting any IEDs along the path they just travelled on:

On Success:

Something about the road feels wrong before anything explodes. The ruts ahead aren’t random—too evenly spaced, looping back toward the shoulder in a way you’ve seen before, once, during training, and again in a grainy after-action slide deck. Daisy-chained. You clock it instantly: multiple charges tied together, laid fast but with intent, designed to hit more than one vehicle and force a halt right here. The realization lands heavy, a cold certainty that this stretch of road isn’t just dangerous—it’s structured.

Your eyes flick to the ground around you, and the picture fills in fast. Shallow disturbances along the verge, wires half-hidden in the dust, the fields beyond offering clear lines of fire. Whoever set this up didn’t rush; they planned for panic and momentum, for vehicles to bunch up, for decisions to be made too late. You haven’t hit it yet—but you’re seconds from where they want you. The ambush isn’t behind you. It’s ahead, waiting for you to commit.

You have just enough time to act. Do you halt and risk being fixed in place? Push through and hope the charges don’t go? Dismount under uncertain fire? Break contact before it’s sprung and leave something unfinished behind you? The pattern is clear now, the trap obvious to anyone who knows what to look for. The question isn’t whether this is an ambush.

On Failure:

The turn back toward CP1 feels rushed even when it isn’t. The road narrows, the fields closing in just enough to make maneuvering feel constrained, and then the world detonates. The blast hits hard and close, the concussion punching through armor and bone alike. Tires shred, antennas whip away, and the convoy lurches to a halt in a cloud of dust and smoke. For a heartbeat, there’s nothing but ringing ears and the taste of grit in your mouth.

Then the gunfire starts, wild and rapid, cutting through the air from open ground beyond the road. It’s inaccurate but relentless, meant to pin and confuse rather than kill outright. You realize quickly that this isn’t the ambush the snipers warned about.

This is something sloppier, faster, meant to force movement rather than finish the fight. Whoever planned this wants you reacting, not thinking, pushing forward, louder and harder, exactly where they want you. The terrain itself seems to conspire with the attackers; shallow ditch lines and low berms create natural channels that subtly guide the convoy along a narrow, covered route. Yet it’s a route fraught with obvious risk, seemingly an invitation for a trap, hinting at the herding tactic at play. A savvy leader would take note of these features, perhaps seeing an opportunity to counter-maneuver against the enemy’s intent.

They entered a hasty @UUID[Compendium.outside-the-wire.macros.Macro.dTM0GJXXQA7VrId8]{IED ambush}.

  • Roll 1d10.

    • 1-3 = Lead Vehicle Hit.

    • 4-6 = Lead + Second Vehicle.

    • 7-9 = Lead, Second, + Third.

    • 10 = All Vehicles Hit

If the leader made a successful Tactics roll, only the first vehicle is affected. Vehicles affected:

  • Surface-laid charges

  • Tires destroyed

  • Antennas stripped

  • Gunners stunned

  • Small arms fire from open ground

Enemy fire is inaccurate—but suppressive.

The ambush is not meant to annihilate. It is meant to force momentum. Your vehicles can roll on run flats forward out of the kill box. The armor has held and will hold against small arms fire. The patrol heavily outguns the insurgents.

There are six regular insurgents caught in caught 30 meters off the road, in the in the middle of a farmer’s cut-up field.

Insurgent Intent

Push the patrol:

  • Faster

  • Louder

  • Toward CP1

  • Into the prepared ambush, the snipers see

With either choice, the players must contend first with the ambush site, phase 6.

Phase 6 begins immediately when any occur:

  • The patrol encounters an IED detonation or effective small-arms fire

  • Vehicles are disabled or halted under fire

  • Snipers report enemy forces actively set and oriented

  • Sunlight Die reaches 6

Do not pause to recap. Do not soften the transition.

The situation collapses inward all at once. Vehicles sit dead or crippled, radios half-working or gone entirely. Someone is shouting over the intercom while someone else stunned, concussed in the back of a truck.

Company A is inbound, but not here yet. The sun climbs higher, burning away the last excuses of darkness, and every second stretches thinner than the last.

This is the moment where the plan ends, and leadership begins. Every option carries weight: push through the fire, break contact and fall back, hold ground and wait, call for fire, and accept what follows. Civilians are nearby—you can feel them even if you can’t see them—and whatever you do will echo beyond this road. There is no clean answer here, no correct path. Only decisions and the consequences that arrive, whether you’re ready for them or not.

The Situation

Vehicles are stopped or slowed.
Fire is inaccurate but suppressive.
Civilians are nearby, unseen but present. The Snipers are isolated and facing a different group of insurgents. Company A is inbound — not here yet. The sun is climbing.

Decision Window (Strict)

  • Start a 90-second real-world timer

  • Players may ask clarifying questions only

  • No tactical rehearsals

  • No multi-branch planning

At the end of 90 seconds:

  • If no decision → [[/tracker "command confidence" -1]]{-1 Command immediately}

  • Patrol Leader must choose anyway

Allowed Orders

(Choose One To The Patrol And One To The Snipers)

The Patrol Leader must issue one primary order:

  1. ASSAULT THROUGH— The players turn their vehicles into the ambush, driving directly at the attackers, to break their will.

  2. BREAK CONTACT & WITHDRAW— The players find a route out of the kill zone, drop smoke to hide their withdrawal, and head to CP1

  3. ANCHOR & HOLD— The players hold their spot, keeping the attackers at a distance, perhaps calling for fire and waiting for Company A.

No hybrids. No sequencing (“we’ll do A then B”).

Snipers are either engaging or remaining hidden — choose.

OPTION: Fast Resolution
(One Roll Only)

Players can roll through a skirmish battle or resolve the chosen order with one roll, using:

  • Tactics → movement, assault, withdrawal

  • Instinct → avoiding catastrophe, reading the trap

  • Fires / Comms → support requests

Apply one DRM only (GM picks the worst applicable).

Results

  • Success

    • Order works as intended

    • Apply one benefit

  • Failure

    • Order partially works

    • Apply one complication + one cost

No rerolls. No prolonged firefights.

Immediate Consequences (Session-Visible)

Apply at least one consequence now, not later:

Choice

Guaranteed Cost

Assault Through

[[/tracker "insurgent activity" -1]]{-1 Insurgent Activity}

Break Contact

[[/tracker "command confidence" -1]]{-1 Command}

Anchor & Hold

[[/tracker "insurgent activity" +1]]{+1 Insurgent Activity}

Call Fires

[[/tracker "local trust" -1]]{Trust -1} (collateral risk)

These apply even on success. War does not reward good decisions.

Sniper Resolution (Fast)

If snipers engage:

  • Surprised, the insurgents flee.

  • Sniper status becomes Compromised

If snipers remain hidden:

  • They survive intact

  • Enemy strength remains higher

The Cavalry
(Failsafe, Not A Reward)

If 3+ Vehicles are Mobility Killed OR the Sunlight Die reaches 10, Company A arrives.

“Shepherd One, Alpha. We have visual. We’re taking control of the battlespace. Pull your people back.”

Then, quietly:

“Good effort. We’ve got it from here.”

Effects:

  • Enemy disengages

  • VIP survives

  • Media / Command scrutiny increases

  • Patrol agency ends

End Condition

Phase 6 ends when any occur:

  • Patrol regains mobility

  • Patrol deliberately withdraws

  • Company A takes control

Immediately move to Fallout.

“Shepherd One, Qalat. Copy end state. Return to base when able. Debrief on arrival.”

End the session once:

  • The patrol regains initiative or

  • Withdraws deliberately or

  • Mission collapses

Resolve consequences on the campaign tracks:

  • Trust: civilian handling

  • Command: mission adherence

  • Insurgent Activity: escalation or disruption

Ask the table:

“Was this worth it?”

Do not answer for them.

GM Notes – Why This Works

  • The civilian dilemma is not a trap; it is a profound element of reality reflecting real-world complexities.

  • The mission can succeed and still feel wrong, underscoring the moral ambiguity of authentic military engagements.

  • Quiet success is real success, highlighting the understated victories that often define true-life operations.

  • Escalation solves today and ruins tomorrow, a truth supported by historical and contemporary conflicts.

  • To deepen the scenario’s realism, consider posing reflective if the players saved the child, have a group of villagers comes by in search of the kid, and they reward the group for saving her. Or if they did not, the players observe a funeral for the child.

Sample debrief questions:

  1. How did your decisions during the scenario reflect your personal values, and how might these decisions differ in a real-life context?

  2. What were the most challenging aspects of the mission, and how did your team address them?

  3. How do you think the presence of civilians in conflict zones affects military operations, and what parallels can you draw with real-world situations?

Optional Extensions

  • Return leg harassment

  • Sniper recovery under daylight

  • Media presence

  • Command scrutiny

  • Local elder confrontation

Only add if time allows.
